newsitem.title: JAPAN: INSTANT VIEW - Japan May current account surplus.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Japan May current account surplus.

text.p: The following is a selection of initial reactions by economists and analysts to Japan's May current account surplus figures, which the Finance Ministry said on Wednesday rose 154.9 percent to 906.8 billion yen.
KENICHI FUTAKAMI, DAIWA BANK RESEARCH INSTITUTE:

"The surplus was in line with our expectations. The surplus is unlikely to keep up its very sharp growth pace in the coming months due to a stronger yen and slow economic growth. For the entire fiscal 1997, the current account surplus will likely show an increase of about 40 percent."

"During April and May, there was a good level of inventories of goods which were used for exports, which in turn pushed up Japan's overall exports during those months. With those inventory levels coming down and prospects of slow growth in consumption, Japanese companies are unlikely to boost their production this year."
CAMERON UMETSU, ASSISTANT DIRECTOR RESEARCH, UBS SECURITIES TOKYO:
"The headline figures are clearly within expectations.

"While we're in the middle of a sustained year-on-year uptrend in Japan's external surpluses, the year-on-year gains should moderate from the third quarter on as import growth gradually picks up. The current account surplus to the GDP ratio would probably stay below two percent in calendar year 1997. So, we're not looking for a runaway external surplus in Japan."

Asked about the implications for the credit market: "I think the reaction should be generally neutral. We see the dollar picking up slightly here, more or less on that the release of the figures weren't even larger than the general expectations. Generally, these numbers were well telegraphed and should really offer no new surprises for the markets."

Asked whether bonds would take heart now from any new gains in the yen: "That's the key wild card for the bond market at this stage of the game. The Ministry of Finance is trying to protect the 110 to 120 (yen) comfort zone and given the currency's proximity to the lower end of that range, the bond market is seeking some solace in the fact that it is one constraint on any near-term BOJ tightening. That's what has supported JGBs in the past few weeks."
CHRIS PAVLOU, TREASURER, GLOBAL MARKETS, MIDLAND BANK TOKYO:
"These figures are good figures...from the market's point of view, from the government's point of view and the currency market as well. So, I expect a neutral situation now."

Pavlou told Reuters Financial Television that the Japanese government probably has a range it wants the yen to trade in. "...The government hasn't told us, but a range of 112 to 117, and maybe a range of 110 to 115. But it must be a very, very comfortable figure for the Ministry of Finance and the BOJ (the Bank of Japan)."
Pavlou said he was not sure if the government would be able to boost domestic demand sufficiently to bring the surplus to below 2.0 percent of GDP.
"I'm not so sure we are going to see this trend in the second half of the year. I think it's going to take a bit of time before that balance comes down to maybe two percent."
